summary: Defines a socket as the unique identifier a message is sent to or from. It is a 32-bit number, with even numbers for receiving sockets and odd ones for sending. The note was written by Joel Winett of Lincoln Laboratory for the network socket committee.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 147 defines a network socket as a 32-bit identifier for a communication endpoint. It describes fields that identify a host, user, and sending or receiving socket.

subtitle: A proposed structure for identifying network sockets and their associated processes.

tldr.problem: Network sockets needed a naming structure that could identify the host and user associated with a connection for communication and accounting.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 147 defines a socket as a 32-bit identifier and describes an 8-bit home field, a 16-bit user field, and an 8-bit tag divided into plug and polarity.
tldr.outcome: RFC 147 updates RFC 129 and describes a socket format implemented in the Lincoln Laboratory 360/67 NCP.

today: RFC 147 updates RFC 129. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces RFC 147.

sections.title: What a Socket Identifies
sections.content:
A socket is the unique identification to or from which information is transmitted in the network. The RFC describes it as a 32-bit number; even sockets identify receiving sockets and odd sockets identify sending sockets. The host where the process runs is also part of the socket's identity.

In this proposal, a socket identifies a port used for machine-to-machine communication through the ARPA Network. Communication takes place from one socket to another, each associated with a process at a known host.
sections.plainLanguage: A socket identifies one end of a network communication. Its number indicates whether it receives or sends, and it is associated with a process on a host.

sections.title: Known and Assigned Socket Names
sections.content:
The RFC says sockets on each host should be associated with a known process or left undefined. Some socket names should be universally known and tied to a process using a specified protocol, such as a logger or file-transfer service.

Other socket names can be supplied in a message sent over a universally known socket, as in the Initial Connection Protocol. The note raises questions about whether socket names should be visible to users and whether a process should reuse the same socket for the same purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Some service sockets have names that every host knows. Other socket names can be sent over a well-known connection when needed.

sections.title: The Suggested Socket Fields
sections.content:
For network accounting, the author says NCPs should record connection times, message and bit counts, hosts, and sockets. To make socket identifiers meaningful, they should identify the user, account, or process.

The proposed 32-bit layout has an 8-bit home field, a 16-bit user field, and an 8-bit tag. The tag contains a 7-bit plug and a one-bit polarity: zero for receive and one for send. The RFC says this layout was implemented in the Lincoln Laboratory 360/67 NCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed number has fields for a host, a user, and a socket tag. The tag includes one bit that marks the socket as receive or send.
